title: Technical Manifesto: Scientific Software Development
text:
Expectation vs. Reality
In scientific research, we often imagine ourselves spending most of our time thinking deeply and understanding complex systems. However, the reality of computational research is often dominated by “plumbing”: managing environments, fighting with SLURM, and debugging boilerplate code.
The goal of this manifesto is to automate the plumbing so you can focus on the science.

title: Technical Manifesto: Scientific Software Development
text:
Opportunity Cost
Investing in modern development practices might feel slow initially, but it prevents the “Conda Hell” and “Terminal Staring” that consume the majority of research time.

Acceleration (JAX / PyTorch)

Rule of Thumb: If it can be done with numpy vectorized operations it will be faster on a GPU
Auto-Diff: Get gradients for ODE or ABM simulations.
Batching: vmap runs 1,000s of simulations in parallel on 1 GPU.
Drop in Replacement: With Jax just replace np with jnp to get immediate hardware accelration.

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import vmap

# A standard function for one data-point
def compute_score(x):
    return jnp.sum(jnp.sin(x) ** 2)

# Automatically vectorize to handle batches
batch_score = vmap(compute_score)

# Result: Instant GPU acceleration for 10,000 samples

title: Supplementary Materials
text:
The folgenden pseudocode describes the bottleneck adapter initialization used in our BERT model:
import torch.nn as nn

class Adapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, adapter_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.down_project = nn.Linear(input_dim, adapter_dim)
        self.act = nn.GELU()
        self.up_project = nn.Linear(adapter_dim, input_dim)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Bottleneck architecture
        residual = x
        x = self.down_project(x)
        x = self.act(x)
        x = self.up_project(x)
        return x + residual

title: Efficient Fine-Tuning with BERT Adapters: A Network Science Perspective
text:
Introduction
Large-scale language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP). However, as mentioned in Devlin et al. (2018), full parameter fine-tuning requires significant computational resources, especially when dealing with domain-specific datasets in fields like Network Science.


Methodology
We utilize the bottleneck architecture described in Houlsby et al. (2019). This approach inserts two modules per transformer layer: one after the multi-head attention and one after the feed-forward layer. Each module consists of a down-projection, a non-linear activation, and an up-projection, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters while maintaining representation quality.


Results and Discussion
Our experiments on the CSDS research dataset indicate that BERT adapters converge faster than full fine-tuning. We find that the structural properties of the attention weights in adapted models exhibit higher modularity compared to their fully fine-tuned counterparts, suggesting that adapters preserve the original model’s “backbone” more effectively.






Figure 1: Figure 1: ROC Curves Across Hyperparameter Sweep. The curves demonstrate the robustness of BERT adapters across different bottleneck dimensions and learning rates. All configurations achieve an AUC > 0.92, with the \(d=512\) configuration showing the fastest convergence.





Conclusion
We have demonstrated that BERT adapters are a highly efficient tool for scientific development in NLP. By minimizing the trainable parameter count, we enable more rapid iteration and experimentation on academic-scale hardware.


References


Devlin, Jacob, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. 2018. “BERT: Pre-Training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1810.04805.


Houlsby, Neil, Andrei Giurgiu, Stanislaw Jastrzebski, Brando Morrone, Quentin Larsson, Mansi Sharma, and Dmitry Kalenichenko. 2019. “Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP.” In International Conference on Machine Learning, 2790–99. PMLR.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
Why This Post Exists
Most of us did not get into research because we love debugging environments, waiting on queues, or fighting invisible data bugs. We got into research because we want to answer hard questions.
Modern scientific work is a software project. Full stop. If your codebase is brittle, your science is brittle. If your workflow is reproducible, your science scales. The degree to which you invest in structure determines whether your future self can trust and extend the work, or will spend a week re-excavating what past-you was thinking.
This post is a practical field guide drawn from a talk: what breaks, what helps, and what I would actually recommend to students trying to do serious technical work in 2026.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
Expectation vs. Reality
The biggest mismatch in scientific programming is not about intelligence or domain knowledge. It is about where the time actually goes.



What I Imagined

data_imagined = [
  {name: "Reading/Understanding", value: 20, color: "#861388"},
  {name: "Thinking Deeply", value: 60, color: "#E15A97"},
  {name: "Writing Code", value: 10, color: "#2F6690"},
  {name: "Communicating", value: 10, color: "#0CBABA"}
]

Plot.plot({
  width: 420,
  height: 360,
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(data_imagined, {
      x: "1",
      y: "value",
      fill: "color",
      stroke: "white",
      title: d => `${d.name}: ${d.value}%`
    }),
    Plot.text(data_imagined, Plot.stackY({
      x: "1",
      y: "value",
      text: d => `${d.name}\n(${d.value}%)`,
      fill: "white",
      fontSize: 12
    }))
  ],
  coordinate: "polar",
  axis: null
})


















What Actually Happened

data_reality = [
  {name: "Reading", value: 10, color: "#861388"},
  {name: "Conda Hell", value: 10, color: "#132a3b"},
  {name: "Actual Algorithm", value: 10, color: "#19374d"},
  {name: "Boilerplate/IO", value: 20, color: "#1f4460"},
  {name: "Off-by-one bugs", value: 10, color: "#29597e"},
  {name: "SLURM Queues", value: 10, color: "#2F6690"},
  {name: "Matplotlib Ticks", value: 10, color: "#4483b3"},
  {name: "Terminal Staring", value: 10, color: "#71a3c9"},
  {name: "Thinking", value: 5, color: "#E15A97"},
  {name: "Making Slides", value: 5, color: "#0CBABA"}
]

Plot.plot({
  width: 420,
  height: 360,
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(data_reality, {
      x: "1",
      y: "value",
      fill: "color",
      stroke: "white",
      title: d => `${d.name}: ${d.value}%`
    }),
    Plot.text(data_reality, Plot.stackY({
      x: "1",
      y: "value",
      text: d => d.value >= 10 ? d.name : "",
      fill: d => ["#71a3c9"].includes(d.color) ? "#2d3436" : "white",
      fontSize: 10
    }))
  ],
  coordinate: "polar",
  axis: null
})


















“Conda Hell” is not a joke. It is a tax levied on anyone who did not invest early in environment hygiene. The lesson is not that software is annoying — the lesson is that if you do not invest in structure up front, the friction compounds. Each unresolved environment issue, each manually re-run cell, each figure you cannot reproduce six months later, is a compounding interest payment on technical debt.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
A Moral Failure





The “world if” meme is funny but the underlying point is serious. Enormous amounts of scientific compute have been consumed not on the science but on the scaffolding — re-running lost experiments, porting code that was never meant to be portable, debugging race conditions in ad-hoc parallel scripts. Without SLURM we would have cured cancer by now (probably not, but the sentiment captures real frustration).
The fix is not to heroically tolerate the friction. It is to reduce it structurally.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
The Iron Rule
There is a tension every researcher hits:

If you take the time to build software the right way, you worry you will never reuse it.
If you write sloppy code, it will eventually bite you.
Damned if you do. Damned if you don’t.

The way out of this dilemma is a calibrated investment in structure — not gold-plating, not cowboy scripts, but just enough that your future self (or a collaborator) can trust and extend the work.
How much structure is “just enough”? The XKCD chart below is a reasonable heuristic:



Is It Worth The Time? (XKCD)


If you will run a task once a week and automation takes a week to build, it pays for itself in two years. If you run it daily and it takes a day to automate, you break even in a month. Most scientific pipelines fall firmly in the “worth automating” zone.

section: The Workflow You Are Actually Building
text:
The Workflow You Are Actually Building
Before diving into specific tools, it helps to be explicit about the shape of the problem:

You have data or simulation parameters.
You have a model — ABM, statistical, or ML.
You want to run sweeps over parameter space with fixed logic.
You want to collect and visualize results without manual copy-paste.
You want to turn plots into a publication or shareable artifact.

The goal is to automate the plumbing so that you can focus on the science. Every hour spent hand-managing results is an hour not spent thinking about what those results mean.

A Concrete Example
To make this tangible, consider a small but realistic pipeline:

Fine-tune a BERT model on AG News (4 classes: World, Sports, Business, Sci/Tech).
Train a lightweight adapter/MLP on extracted embeddings.
Run parameter sweeps over adapter dimension and learning rate.
Compare results and publish figures automatically.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
The Foundation

1. Keep Core Logic in Python Source
Notebooks are excellent for exploration. They are poor as the only source of truth for production logic. If your model or simulation lives only in a .ipynb, it is not testable, not importable, and nearly impossible to version cleanly.
The pattern is: write the core logic in .py files in a src/ directory, then import it into notebooks for exploration and into scripts for batch runs.
Type annotations are not just documentation. They are the interface contract between components, and they are what let a static analysis tool (or an LLM) reason about your code accurately.


2. Reproducible Environments with uv
uv is significantly faster than conda and produces exact lockfiles that make environments reproducible across machines — including HPC clusters. The core concept is simple: declare your dependencies in pyproject.toml, commit the uv.lock file, and anyone with uv installed gets an identical environment.
[project]
name = "scientific_dev"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "jax>=0.9.0",
    "snakemake>=8.4.0",
    "pydantic>=2.12.5",
]
Linked dependencies also prevent identical binaries from being duplicated across environments, which matters when disk quotas are tight on shared HPC systems.


3. Hardware Acceleration with JAX / PyTorch
The rule of thumb: if your computation can be expressed as vectorized operations over arrays, it will run faster on a GPU. The jump in throughput for embarrassingly parallel workloads — parameter sweeps, ensemble simulations, batch inference — is typically one to two orders of magnitude.
JAX is particularly well-suited to scientific computing because it supports automatic differentiation through arbitrary programs, including ODE solvers and agent-based models. vmap turns a function over one data point into a function over a batch, with no manual batching logic:
PyTorch is the default for neural networks and has a larger ecosystem of pretrained models. For custom simulations or differentiable physics, JAX is often the better fit.


4. Validation with Pydantic
Ad-hoc config dictionaries are a silent source of bugs. A typo in a key, a float where an int is expected, a missing required field — all of these can propagate deep into a run before surfacing. Pydantic catches them at construction time.
Validated schemas also have a second benefit in 2026: LLMs can read a Pydantic model and generate valid configurations, valid test fixtures, and accurate documentation without guessing at the types. Structured code is LLM-legible code.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
The Plumbing

1. Command Layer with just
just is a command runner that acts as a project-wide vocabulary of tasks. Instead of each collaborator needing to remember the exact flags for snakemake or quarto, they run just all or just preview. It also enforces that everyone runs tasks in the same environment.
# Run the full pipeline (local profile, baseline config)
all p="local" c="configs/nlp_baseline.yaml":
    uv run snakemake --workflow-profile ./workflow/profiles/{{p}} --configfile {{c}}

# Preview the Quarto site locally
preview:
    cd notebooks/quarto && quarto preview . --no-browser
View Justfile →


2. Orchestration with Snakemake
Snakemake is a workflow manager that automatically determines what needs to run based on what already exists. If a model checkpoint is present, it skips training and goes straight to evaluation. If you add a new config, it runs only the missing experiments. This “amnesia proof” property is critical for large sweeps where some runs succeed and others fail.
It also integrates natively with SLURM, so a local run and a cluster run use the same workflow definition — only the profile changes.
View Full Rule →


3. Testing and CI
A test suite is not bureaucracy. It is the thing that tells you, in thirty seconds, whether the change you just made broke something downstream. For scientific code, the most valuable tests are often not unit tests of individual functions but integration tests that check the full pipeline on a small synthetic dataset.
CI runs those tests on every push, so breakage surfaces in the branch, not in the final writeup week.
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: uv run pytest tests/
View CI Workflow →


4. Experiment Tracking with WandB
Once sweeps exceed more than a handful of runs, you need somewhere to store metrics that is not a directory of CSV files. WandB logs metrics in real time, versions every run, and makes it trivial to compare runs across dimensions.
The config=self.config.model_dump() pattern is where Pydantic and WandB meet: every hyperparameter is automatically logged without manual bookkeeping, and every run is reproducible because the config is versioned alongside the weights.
View Trainer →


5. Storage and Querying with Parquet + DuckDB
Parquet files are the right format for scientific results: columnar, compressed, and queryable with SQL via DuckDB without loading everything into memory. DuckDB’s glob syntax lets you query entire result directories as if they were a single table.
SELECT s.*, m."test/auroc"
FROM read_parquet('results/**/training_stats.parquet') s
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('results/**/test_metrics.parquet') m
  ON s.full_run_name = m.full_run_name
For projects with more relational structure, SQLModel provides a type-safe Python ORM on top of a conventional database.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
Why Quarto Matters
Quarto is not just a rendering tool. It is the integration layer where analysis, narrative, equations, and interactivity can live in one reproducible artifact.
The typical alternative is a patchwork: a Jupyter notebook for analysis, a separate LaTeX file for the paper, figures exported manually and embedded as static images. Every time results change, you update three things and hope they stay in sync. Quarto collapses this into one source of truth. The notebook that generated the figure is the document. It is harder to misplace a figure or lose a parameter setting when the notebook that generated it is the document.
It also supports multiple output formats from the same source — HTML, PDF, revealjs slides, Word — which matters when you need to hand the same content to a conference, a collaborator, and a journal.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
AI Tools for Students
Two categories are worth calling out explicitly:
IDEs with integrated AI assistance:

VSCode — the standard; integrates with Copilot and Claude
Cursor — free for students; strong multi-file context
Project IDX / Antigravity — agent-native workspace

LLMs as high-context research partners:

Gemini Pro — 2M token context; good for large codebases
GitHub Copilot — free for students via GitHub Education
Claude Campus — available with campus credits

The key word in all of these is partner, not replacement. An LLM cannot tell you whether your experimental design has a confound, whether your loss curve looks right, or whether your evaluation metric is appropriate for your task. Those judgments require domain expertise. What an LLM can do is eliminate the time spent on boilerplate, configuration, and lookup — which, as the pie chart above shows, is a substantial fraction of a researcher’s actual hours.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
What I’d Tell a Student

Build one reproducible pipeline end-to-end before optimizing anything. Optimization on a fragile foundation just makes the fragility faster.
Keep your core logic in modules, not only notebooks. If you cannot import it, you cannot test it. If you cannot test it, you cannot trust it.
Let CI catch failures early rather than during the final writeup. A failing test at 2pm on a Tuesday is a minor annoyance. The same failure discovered the night before a submission deadline is a crisis.
Use LLMs as force multipliers, not as replacements for scientific judgment. They are excellent at boilerplate, configuration, and lookup. They cannot tell you whether your experimental design is valid.

title: There is Plenty of Room in Latent Space
text:
Closing
We are a few years — maybe less — until the tools turn substantially more autonomous. The question is not whether to adopt them, but whether the codebase you hand to a more capable agent is something it can work with.
Brittle notebooks, implicit state, hard-coded paths, and untested logic are not just inconvenient for human collaborators. They are opaque to AI collaborators too. The virtuous cycle only closes if the code is structured well enough for the tool to understand it.
The future is not that AI replaces scientific programming. The future is that scientific programming becomes more ambitious because the fixed costs of good engineering drop. That only works if we still care about validation, reproducibility, and clarity.
Let the tools remove friction. Keep your scientific standards high. And maybe, with the time saved, we can cure cancer after all.
